newsitem.title: ROMANIA: TREATMENT OF GYPSIES HURTS ROMANIA EU BID-OFFICIAL.
newsitem.headline: TREATMENT OF GYPSIES HURTS ROMANIA EU BID-OFFICIAL.

text.p: European officials and Gypsy leaders on Tuesday urged Romania to take measures to stop discrimination and violence against Gypsies, cited by the European Union as a hurdle to the country's membership bid.

"Despite positive developments, the situation of the Roma (Gypsies) is still a weak point in Romania," Steffen Skovmand, a member of the European Commission's delegation in Romania, told a news conference.
Skovmand said the European Commission's report on EU enlargement highlighted concerns over treatment of Gypsies in east European countries seeking admission.
Last month, the Commission recommmended that the EU should start membership talks only with five East European countries -- Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic, Slovenia and Estonia.
Its report said only Slovakia failed to qualify for admission on political grounds. Other states generally met requirements except for their treatment of the Roma minority.

Romania, home to one of the largest Gypsy communities in eastern Europe, was passed over. The report praised Romania's progress in implementing democratic reforms, including treatment of its large Hungarian minority, since centrists ousted ex-communists in last year's elections.
"The Roma (Gypsies) represent between five and 15 percent of the population in many countries of the region," said leading Romanian Gypsy rights activist Nicolae Gheorghe.
"In their daily life, they are subject to harassment and aggression. Public opinion should understand that Romania can join Europe only if it solves the plight of our minority."
Gheorge said there was no reliable data throughout Eastern Europe on the Gypsy communities' labour, health and education.

He cited violence against Gypsies by "skinhead" youth gangs in the Czech Republic, police brutality against Gypsies in Romania and Bulgaria, and labour and education discrimination against Gypsies in Hungary. Most violence went unpunished.

A post-communist census shows some 400,000 Gypsies live in Romania. But the European Commission's report quotes Romanian Gypsy leaders as saying that the figure is up to 1.5 million, or seven percent of the population.

Romania's police chief, General Pavel Abraham told reporters there was no systematic police clampdown against Gypsies. "There's no state policy in Romania of discriminating against any minority whatsoever," he said.
Gheorghe called on media to stop portraying Gypsies as trouble-makers and criminals and on courts to be more lenient.
He said courts had delivered two verdicts of suspended jail terms in 37 post-communist attacks in Romania, in which Gypsy homes were gutted and they were driven from their villages.
"We want a strong, clear political signal that this is unacceptable," Gheorghe said.
